doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: British views of America
summary: Light talk on the US election, Clinton, American fast food and the special relationship.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: In a broader sense I’m interested in what Britain thinks of the United States as a whole? How do they look at our last November’s mess with the election?

Well I think we think that was laughable. It got a lot of space. But we think that Clinton’s escapades were grotesque really. So you know, I don’t think the great British public would have too strong an opinion either way. They’d say they’re all a bunch of rogues and vagabonds. They don’t feel much different about our own politicians to be honest. So I don’t think that did America any favors, let’s put it that way. But the extent of American influence is very considerable. Obviously films, certainly T.V., and a lot of American lifestyle aspects, you know, the dreaded fast food for instance, plenty of that.
McDonald’s on every corner? © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-
For sure. There’ll be a thousand outlets by the end of next year I think in Britain. That’s a lot, isn’t it?

About 999 too many perhaps. No I think there’s always, look, there is what is called a special relationship. We are close to each other in many ways. That’s not to say that we think alike. George Bernard Shaw said, “Two nations divided by a common language,” and there is still something of that. But I think we feel pretty comfortable with the relationship I guess.
